quote: to early October in small, cold water tributaries to the Metolius River
note: PDF page (executive summary, no printed number). Adfluvial and fluvial spawners together. No width given. Spawning tributaries named in the report: Jack, Canyon, Roaring, Candle, Jefferson creeks, Whitewater River, plus spring areas of the Metolius mainstem (Heising Spring; near Jack Creek mouth, p. 28).

quote: Monitoring of tributaries using McNeil core samplers showed the spawning gravel is dominated by material 8-32 mm in diameter
note: McNeil core samples from spawning areas: the dominant size class, not a preference or limit. Same page: fines <6.4 mm were 22-33 % of spawning-area gravel in four creeks.

quote: In all spawning streams, temperatures fell below 9°C before spawning began
note: Observed onset condition in every monitored spawning stream; repeated on p. 37. Agrees with the 9 C threshold in mcphail_baxter1996 (p. i).

quote: Summer water temperatures in the streams used by bull trout for spawning and rearing were strongly influenced by cold springs
note: Groundwater/spring influence (the vocabulary has no groundwater variable). Same page: Roaring and Candle creeks 4-6 C in summer. p. 6: no perennial cold spring areas suitable for spawning exist in the mainstem Crooked River, where no spawning was ever documented. Migratory population: mostly adfluvial (Lake Billy Chinook), part fluvial.

quote: Bull trout spawning and juvenile rearing are usually closely associated with cold water systems draining from higher elevations
note: Footnote 11, given as the reason the Pack River watershed was rated low potential for spawning ('predominately low elevation drainage areas', same page) and left out of the aerial redd surveys. No elevation value.

quote: much higher densities of juvenile bull trout have been observed above areas of difficult passage (chutes, bedrock canyons) compared to downstream areas
cited_source: Bustard and Schell 2002; Decker and Hagen 2007
note: Fluvial and adfluvial streams: spawners pass chutes and bedrock canyons to reach natal reaches above them; the authors suggest difficult access gives BT a competitive advantage over rainbow trout and steelhead. No gradient value; chutes/canyons read as steep passage.

quote: In the experience of the authors, redds of large-bodied, migratory Bull Trout have been found in stream sections as small as 2 m wetted width
note: Smallest stream with redds in the authors' experience; such streams held a small share of a population's redds (e.g. Thutade Lake watershed, Hagen 2000). Same lead author as the hagen_etal2015 2 m row (p. 23): not independent.

quote: Depths at redd locations average 24-58 cm, and appear to always be less than 90 cm, while velocities average 14-52 cm/s and are typically 65 cm/s or less
note: Range of study means at redds, 'reviewed in Baxter and McPhail 1996'. The source gives cm; the gate has no cm-to-m rescale for depth. roberge_etal2002 (p. 80) cites the same review as 30-60 cm.

quote: Depths at redd locations average 24-58 cm, and appear to always be less than 90 cm, while velocities average 14-52 cm/s and are typically 65 cm/s or less
note: Redd depths 'appear to always be less than 90 cm'. The source gives cm; the gate has no cm-to-m rescale for depth.

quote: Depths at redd locations average 24-58 cm, and appear to always be less than 90 cm, while velocities average 14-52 cm/s and are typically 65 cm/s or less
note: Range of study means at redds. Matches roberge_etal2002 (p. 80, 0.14-0.52 m/s) from the same review.

quote: Depths at redd locations average 24-58 cm, and appear to always be less than 90 cm, while velocities average 14-52 cm/s and are typically 65 cm/s or less
note: 'Typically 65 cm/s or less': a typical upper value, not an absolute limit.

region: Omineca core area (Williston Reservoir watershed), BC
quote: The largest Bull Trout populations of the Omineca core area spawn in pristine headwater reaches exhibiting stable, clear flows and clean, unembedded gravel-cobble-boulder substrates
note: Large-bodied migratory spawners (Carruthers Creek, upper Osilinka River, Lay Creek). Restated from hagenj_spendlowi_2019 (p. 30).

region: Omineca, Mesilinka and Osilinka river watersheds, BC
quote: in all three systems 1 or 2 smaller populations of large-bodied spawners were identified in shorter, steeper tributaries located close to the reservoir
note: Large-bodied (adfluvial) spawners in steeper tributaries, e.g. Big Creek index section: 'relatively steep, high energy stream', 26 redds on foot (p. 18). No gradient value. The larger populations spawn in pristine upper reaches (same page).

quote: The distribution of Bull Trout redds within a watershed is not random and appears to be strongly related to water temperature (or proxies like elevation), migration barriers, and geomorphology (particularly the presence of alluvial stream sections where spawning gravel accumulations and groundwater exchange are present)
cited_source: Graham et al. 1981; Baxter 1997; Baxter and Hauer 2000; Williamson 2006
note: Elevation as a proxy for water temperature. No value.

quote: The distribution of Bull Trout redds within a watershed is not random and appears to be strongly related to water temperature (or proxies like elevation), migration barriers, and geomorphology (particularly the presence of alluvial stream sections where spawning gravel accumulations and groundwater exchange are present)
cited_source: Graham et al. 1981; Baxter 1997; Baxter and Hauer 2000; Williamson 2006
note: 'Alluvial stream sections' with gravel accumulation and groundwater exchange, read as unconfined valley segments; the source names no valley-width measure or value.

quote: Spawning areas are often associated with cold-water springs, groundwater infiltration, and the coldest streams in a given watershed
cited_source: Pratt 1992; Rieman and McIntyre 1993; Rieman et al. 1997; Baxter and McPhail 1999; Baxter et al. 1999
note: Groundwater/spring association (the vocabulary has no groundwater variable). Same plan p. 6: 'Redds are often constructed in stream reaches fed by springs or near other sources of cold groundwater'.

quote: Preferred spawning habitat consists of low-gradient stream reaches with loose, clean gravel (Fraley and Shepard 1989) and water temperatures of 5 to 9 degrees Celsius
note: 'In late summer to early fall'. Same page gives spawning temperatures 'generally range from 4 to 10' C (Howell et al. 2010); the 2010 critical habitat rule (p. 63930) attributes 4-10 C to Goetz 1989 instead. The low-gradient clause is the same claim as the 2010 rule's gradient row (Fraley and Shepard 1989), so no separate row.

quote: abundance of bull trout redds (spawning areas) was positively correlated with the extent of bounded alluvial valley reaches, which are likely areas of groundwater to surface water exchange
note: Bounded alluvial valley reaches read as unconfined segments; no valley-width value. The plan cites Baxter and McPhail 1999; the Swan River work is cited elsewhere as Baxter and Hauer 2000 (hagen_sary2023 p. 4; the 2010 rule p. 63930, hyporheic flow). Attribution not checked against either paper.

quote: Stream-resident populations are associated with headwater streams in mountainous regions where year-round cold water and velocity or other movement barriers are common. Typically, these streams are smaller and have higher gradients than those occupied by adfluvial and fluvial populations
cited_source: McPhail and Baxter 1996; Mullan et al. 1992
note: Stream-resident populations, all life stages ('Juvenile and adult resident bull trout inhabit the spawning and rearing areas year round', same page). Restates mcphail_baxter1996 p. 12 (already a resident rearing row): not independent. No value.

region: Coterminous United States (review); original Flathead, Montana
quote: The preferred spawning habitat of bull trout consists of low-gradient stream reaches with loose, clean gravel
note: No value. The 2015 recovery plan (p. 6) repeats it. The rule declines to set ranges for its PCEs because 'stream flow and substrate size and composition are influenced by stream order and gradient' (p. 63931).

quote: spawning generally initiated when water temperatures dropped below 10 °C
note: Onset of spawning. mcphail_baxter1996 and hagen_weber2019 cite Fraley and Shepard 1989 (with McPhail and Murray 1979) for 9 C; this rule cites them for 10 C.

quote: Goetz (1989, pp. 22–32) reported a spawning temperature range from 4 to 10 °C
note: Same sentence: 'the range could be wider in some areas (Howell et al. 2010, p. 102)'. The 2015 recovery plan (p. 6) gives 4-10 C citing Howell et al. 2010 and 5-9 C citing Goetz 1989.

quote: Water temperatures of 1.2 to 5.4 °C (34.2 to 41.7 °F) have been reported for incubation
cited_source: Fraley and Shepard 1989; McPhail and Baxter 1996
note: Same sentence: optimum (best embryo survival) 2-4 C, as in the existing mcphail_baxter1996 incubation row.
